b: This article was updated 6.30pm on November 23, to include criticism of Steamforged from Terra Mystica publisher Feuerland Spiele.

Steamforged Games says it is in “positive” talks with a potential investor amid unveiling an £8.6m annual loss – while its auditors warn they have been “unable to determine whether the company will be able to generate sufficient cash flows to meet its liabilities”.

The UK-based publisher, which made a name converting high-profile video game IPs to the tabletop, has faced mounting criticism from crowdfunding backers in recent months over unresolved refunds and dwindling updates across its undelivered projects – which raised almost £19m including late pledges.

That criticism was added to today by Terra Mystica publisher Feuerland Spiele, which said it had “lost trust” in Steamforged over its handling of the £1m Terra Mystica Special Edition crowdfunding campaign, and fears the game may never be delivered.

Steamforged’s accounts for the year to March 2025 – finally published today, almost five months after their filing deadline – reveal a 23% fall in revenue to £10.4m, a 71% plunge in cash reserves to £1.1m and a heavy rise in net liabilities, from £5m to £13.6m.

That sharp financial deterioration was accompanied by Steamforged’s auditors, Sumer Auditco, saying they could not determine whether the company could generate sufficient cash to meet liabilities and continue operating as a going concern.
They found that Steamforged’s trading performance since March 2025 had been “substantially below forecast levels”, with “losses being incurred rather than the profits anticipated”.

Those concerns contributed to the auditors taking the serious step of issuing a “disclaimer of opinion” on the accounts – meaning they were unable to obtain sufficient evidence to determine whether the financial statements prepared by Steamforged’s directors presented a true and fair picture of the business.

A disclaimer of opinion is one of the most serious outcomes of a financial audit, issued when auditors are unable to obtain sufficient evidence to form an opinion on a company’s accounts and believe the potential impact of undetected misstatements could be both “material and pervasive”, according to the Financial Reporting Council’s auditing standards – although it does not necessarily mean the accounts are inaccurate, or that the company is insolvent.

The auditors also said they were unable to verify the valuation of £1.6m in remaining intellectual property assets – principally trademarks – because the directors’ assessment of their value relied on future sales forecasts which had already proved unreliable. They could not determine whether further write-downs were necessary, and were also unable to establish whether adequate accounting records had been maintained.

The newly-published accounts represent a significant escalation in the financial concerns surrounding Steamforged, which cut about a third of its workforce earlier this year as it moved to reduce its reliance on board game crowdfunding and concentrate on the growth of its Warmachine miniatures business.

Much of its £8.6m loss in the 2024/25 financial year came from £5.7m in exceptional charges relating to the reduced value of IP, game development costs and equipment – but the publisher also recorded a £2.9m operating loss before those charges, compared with a £1.3m operating profit the previous year.

The accounts reveal that Steamforged has decided to discontinue an unspecified number of games and product lines after their sales either stopped altogether, fell significantly or continued at levels which were no longer commercially viable. Those decisions, made after the March 2025 year-end, were cited as further evidence for the write-down of development costs and equipment.

The publisher’s crowdfunding revenue fell 38% to £5.35m, with Steamforged blaming fewer campaign launches, delays to planned releases and weaker demand in parts of the tabletop market. Direct sales revenue edged up from £4.86m to £5.08m, but higher production and shipping costs across the business pushed its gross profit margin down from 38.9% to 27.1%.

The scale of Steamforged’s financial difficulties had already been flagged earlier this year by investor Foresight, which slashed the valuation of its holdings in the company by almost 74% during the first half of 2026, from £3.68m to just over £960,000, across two of its investment vehicles.

Foresight, which invested £5m in Steamforged in 2019 across three funds, said in June that the publisher had suffered “a few disappointing crowdfunding campaigns over the last 12 months” and was looking to shift towards its higher-margin Iron Kingdoms business, which includes Warmachine.
Steamforged has not launched a new crowdfunding campaign since Terra Mystica Special Edition, which raised just over £1m in November last year.

Terra Mystica publisher Feuerland Spiele publicly criticised Steamforged today, saying it had repeatedly been assured that this year’s redundancies and restructuring would not affect the game’s special edition, which was originally scheduled for delivery in April 2027.
It said a promised campaign update had remained unpublished for several weeks, despite Feuerland having already seen a draft.
“As a result, we have lost trust in Steamforged,” Feuerland said. “Unfortunately, we share the concern of some backers that the Terra Mystica Special Edition will never see the light of day.”

Feuerland stressed that Steamforged alone had collected the campaign funding, but said the situation was already damaging its own reputation and affecting perceptions of its separate Gamefound campaign for The Danes.
“We put our reputation in other hands and while Steamforged alone collected the funding, this situation is already damaging our brand,” it said.

The accounts show Steamforged had about £12.4m in deferred crowdfunding revenue at the end of March 2025, up from £11.8m a year earlier, reflecting money received for projects for which the company had yet to meet its obligations. About £9.3m of that amount was classified in the report as falling beyond the subsequent 12 months.

Despite its cutback in new board game crowdfunding activity, Steamforged’s latest financial forecasts still factor in receipts from future campaigns – although its co-founders and directors Rich Loxam and Mat Hart acknowledge that both the timing and amount of that income remain uncertain.
The newly-published accounts also reveal that Steamforged is in discussions with an unnamed investor over additional funding for its operations and future growth.
Loxam and Hart said those discussions had “progressed positively”, but acknowledged that no binding agreement had been reached and there was no certainty a transaction would go ahead.

The pair nevertheless maintained that Steamforged could continue operating as a going concern, citing its future trading plans, ongoing financial support from parent company Steamforged Holdings and the prospect of securing new investment.
The accounts show Steamforged owed fellow group companies £3m in March 2025 – a figure which has remained virtually unchanged since March 2023.

Steamforged Holdings has repeatedly indicated it will not seek repayment until the publisher’s cash flow allows – an assurance the directors have relied on in their assessments of Steamforged’s ability to continue operating for at least the past two years.
The financial uncertainty also comes amid a major shake-up of parent business Steamforged Holdings, which has lost four of its seven directors since July – three of those since the start of November.

Those departures were Robert Michael Jones, an investment manager associated with Foresight who served as an investor director at Steamforged, former Steamforged commercial director Toby Davies, who joined Tycoon Games, games industry veteran Ron Ashtiani and Xiaowen Guan.
The changes leave Loxam, Hart and Simon Spalding, a former Hasbro and DreamWorks executive, as the holding company’s only remaining directors. The reasons for the departures have not been disclosed.
Steamforged’s long-delayed account filing comes as the publisher continues to face backer unrest over the delivery of a string of multimillion-pound crowdfunding projects.
The largest is Monster Hunter World: Iceborne, which raised almost £6.3m including late pledges from close to 15,000 backers, and was originally expected to be delivered in November 2024.

Steamforged said in January this year that it was aiming to deliver the game to all regions by July, but has provided just two campaign updates since – the latter, in July, apologising for the lack of communication and saying it was waiting for information from partners before it could provide a concrete fulfilment update. No further update has been posted.

Outstanding projects span the £3.2m Helldivers 2 campaign, the £1.8m-raising Elden Ring: Rot & Sorcery and £1.2m Hearts of Iron: The Board Game, whose IP owner Paradox Interactive confirmed to BoardGameWire last month that it was in discussions with Steamforged about how to get the project completed.

Its other unfulfilled campaigns include the US production and shipping of Horizon Forbidden West: Seeds of Rebellion and Euthia: Cruel Frost, both of which were postponed due to tariffs uncertainty last year, and the second wave of its P3 Paints crowdfund, which has been delayed by up to a year due to a production issue with the metallic colours.

BoardGameWire reported in October that backers across several campaigns had complained about waiting weeks or months for responses to refund requests, with some turning to PayPal disputes and credit card chargebacks to recover their money.

Steamforged has continued delivering some projects, including non-US fulfilment of Horizon Forbidden West: Seeds of Rebellion and Euthia: Cruel Frost, as well as the pre-order campaign for 6: Siege – The Board Game, which it acquired from collapsed publisher Mythic Games.
But the redundancies and subsequent reduction in communication have raised concerns among backers about whether the publisher has the resources needed to complete its remaining projects.

Steamforged told BoardGameWire in June that the “vast majority” of creative work on its crowdfunded board games was complete and that it retained the internal resources and external capabilities needed to fulfil its commitments.
The publisher also said revenue from Warmachine and P3 Paints had tripled over the preceding 21 months, with production capacity expanded substantially to meet demand.

BoardGameWire made repeated attempts to contact CEO Rich Loxam across August, September and October about unresolved refunds, delivery schedules and the impact of the redundancies on Steamforged’s outstanding projects, without receiving a response.

Speaking to BoardGameWire during the Terra Mystica Special Edition campaign in November last year, Loxam said Steamforged had never failed to deliver a crowdfunding project in more than a decade of running campaigns.
He also said the publisher had strong retail and distribution channels, adding that “we’re not dependent on crowdfunding to survive”.
BoardGameWire has approached Steamforged for comment following the new accounts filing, and will update this article or run a new piece if we receive a reply.
